questions.enonce_markdown:
The energy cycle below represents the enthalpy changes involved in the formation of solid sodium chloride.

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

(i) Identify the enthalpy changes involved in steps A, B, C and D.

(ii) Calculate the enthalpy change of formation of $\mathrm{NaCl_{(s)}}$ *[5 marks]*

*Values printed on the figure:* A $= +108.3$, B $= +500$, C $= +121$, D $= -364$ and E $= -776$ (all in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The enthalpy changes.**

| Step | Process | Name of the enthalpy change | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na(g)}$ | **Enthalpy of atomisation** (sublimation) **of sodium** | $+108.3\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| B | $\mathrm{Na(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+(g)} + e^-$ | **First ionisation enthalpy (energy) of sodium** | $+500\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| C | $\tfrac12\mathrm{Cl_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl(g)}$ | **Enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine** (half the Cl-Cl bond dissociation enthalpy) | $+121\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| D | $\mathrm{Cl(g)} + e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl^-(g)}$ | **First electron affinity of chlorine** | $-364\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ |

(Step E, not asked, is the **lattice enthalpy of formation** of sodium chloride: $\mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$, $-776\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.)

**(ii) Enthalpy change of formation.** By Hess's law, the enthalpy change of the direct route ($\Delta H_f^\circ$ from the elements $\mathrm{Na(s)} + \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}$ to $\mathrm{NaCl(s)}$) equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the route that goes round the cycle (steps A, B, C, D, then E):

$$\Delta H_f^\circ = \Delta H_A + \Delta H_B + \Delta H_C + \Delta H_D + \Delta H_E$$

$$\Delta H_f^\circ = (+108.3) + (+500) + (+121) + (-364) + (-776) = -410.7\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$$

The enthalpy change of formation of sodium chloride is **$-410.7\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$** (about $-411\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$): the formation is exothermic.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define the following terms as applied to solid state chemistry.

A: Crystal lattice

B: Unit cell

(ii) Draw the unit cell of sodium chloride (NaCl). *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

**A. Crystal lattice:** the regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of the particles (atoms, ions or molecules) of a crystalline solid, in which each particle (lattice point) has the same surroundings.

**B. Unit cell:** the smallest repeating part (a small block) of the crystal lattice which, when repeated in all three directions in space, builds up the whole lattice.

**(ii) Unit cell of sodium chloride.** It is a **cube** in which the chloride ions $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ occupy the corners and the centres of the six faces (a face-centred cubic arrangement), and the sodium ions $\mathrm{Na^+}$ occupy the middle of each of the 12 edges and the centre of the cube. Each ion has 6 nearest neighbours of opposite charge (**6 : 6 co-ordination**), so the ions alternate along every row, column and diagonal of the cube.

The cube is drawn as three layers (looking from above), each a $3\times3$ grid of positions; the layers at $z = 0$ and $z = 1$ (bottom and top faces) are identical:

```
Bottom and top faces        Middle layer (half way up)

Cl-   Na+   Cl-             Na+   Cl-   Na+
Na+   Cl-   Na+             Cl-   Na+   Cl-
Cl-   Na+   Cl-             Na+   Cl-   Na+
```

Number of ions belonging to one unit cell: $\mathrm{Cl^-}$: $8\times\tfrac18$ (corners) $+ 6\times\tfrac12$ (faces) $= 4$; $\mathrm{Na^+}$: $12\times\tfrac14$ (edges) $+ 1$ (centre) $= 4$. The unit cell therefore contains **4 formula units of NaCl**, in the ratio 1 : 1.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Give one similarity and one difference between a chemical bond and an intermolecular force.

Similarity:

Difference:

(ii) List and locate all the types of bonds in solid $(\mathrm{NH_4})_3\mathrm{PO_4}$ *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** *Similarity:* both are **electrostatic** in origin: they result from the attraction between opposite charges (full charges for ions, partial charges for polar molecules, or temporary and induced charges).

*Difference:* a chemical bond is **much stronger** (typically about $150$ to $1000\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) than an intermolecular force (about $1$ to $40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$). A chemical bond holds atoms or ions together *within* a compound (it is broken in a chemical reaction), whereas intermolecular forces act *between* separate molecules and are overcome when a substance melts or boils.

**(ii)** Solid ammonium phosphate is an ionic compound made of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ and $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ ions. The types of bonds and their locations:

- **Ionic (electrovalent) bonds:** electrostatic attraction between the ammonium ions $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ and the phosphate ions $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ throughout the crystal lattice (three $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ for each $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$).
- **Covalent bonds (shared pair of electrons):** the N-H bonds *inside* each $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ ion (three of the four N-H bonds), and the P-O bonds *inside* each $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ ion.
- **Dative (co-ordinate) covalent bonds:** the fourth N-H bond of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ (the lone pair of nitrogen of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is donated to $\mathrm{H^+}$), and the P$\rightarrow$O bond(s) in $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ in which both electrons of the shared pair come from phosphorus; once formed, all four N-H bonds are identical.
- **Hydrogen bonds:** between a hydrogen atom of an $\mathrm{N{-}H}$ group of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ and an oxygen atom of a neighbouring $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ ion ($\mathrm{N{-}H\cdots O}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram of vapour pressure against composition for mixtures of propan-1-ol and methylbenzene at constant temperature is given below:

![fig-2](gce-al-chemistry-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_2.png)

What do the curves A to D represent?

A:

B:

C:

D:
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the diagram the vertical axis is the vapour pressure at constant temperature and the horizontal axis is the composition, from 100 % propan-1-ol (left) to 100 % methylbenzene (right). The two dash-dot straight lines (unlabelled) are the **ideal** partial vapour pressures given by Raoult's law, $p_i = x_i\,p_i^{\circ}$.

| Curve | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **A** | The **total vapour pressure of the real mixture** ($p_{\text{total}}$ = sum of the two partial pressures). It lies **above** the ideal straight line and passes through a **maximum**. |
| **B** | The **total vapour pressure of an ideal mixture**: the straight line joining the vapour pressures of the two pure liquids (Raoult's law obeyed). |
| **C** | The **partial vapour pressure of methylbenzene** in the real mixture: it rises from zero (100 % propan-1-ol) to the vapour pressure of pure methylbenzene (100 % methylbenzene), above its ideal straight line. |
| **D** | The **partial vapour pressure of propan-1-ol** in the real mixture: it falls from the vapour pressure of pure propan-1-ol (100 % propan-1-ol) to zero (100 % methylbenzene), above its ideal straight line. |

Interpretation: all the real curves lie above the Raoult's law lines, so the mixture shows a **positive deviation** from Raoult's law. In pure propan-1-ol the molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds; the non-polar methylbenzene breaks some of them and the propan-1-ol/methylbenzene attractions are weaker than the attractions in the pure liquids, so each liquid escapes more easily than in an ideal mixture.

questions.enonce_markdown: Give two properties of a mixture which deviates negatively from Raoult's Law *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a mixture with a **negative deviation**, the attractions between unlike molecules (A-B) are **stronger** than those between like molecules (A-A and B-B). Two properties (any two of the following, each with its reason):

1. **The vapour pressure is lower than that predicted by Raoult's law** (the total vapour pressure curve lies below the ideal straight line and may pass through a minimum), because the stronger A-B attractions make it harder for molecules to escape from the liquid. As a consequence the **boiling point is higher** than that of an ideal mixture and a **maximum boiling point (constant boiling) azeotrope** can form (for example hydrochloric acid / water, or nitric acid / water).
2. **The enthalpy of mixing is negative:** mixing is **exothermic** (heat is given out and the temperature of the mixture rises), because the A-B interactions formed release more energy than is needed to break the A-A and B-B interactions.
3. **The volume of the mixture is smaller than the sum of the volumes of the pure liquids** (volume contraction on mixing, $\Delta V_{\text{mix}} < 0$), because the molecules pack more closely.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the following redox potentials.

$$\mathrm{I_2(aq)} + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{I^-(aq)} \qquad E^\circ = +0.54\ \mathrm{V}$$

$$\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}(aq)} + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}(aq)} \qquad E^\circ = +0.10\ \mathrm{V}$$

(i) Select the species which is the strongest.

A: reducing agent

B: oxidising agent

(ii) Write the cell diagram when the two half cells are coupled and calculate the e.m.f of the cell.

Cell diagram:

Cell e.m.f.: *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The more negative (less positive) the electrode potential, the more readily the reduced form gives up electrons; the more positive the potential, the more readily the oxidised form gains electrons.

- **A. Strongest reducing agent: $\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}$** (thiosulphate ion). It is the reduced form of the couple with the lower $E^\circ$ ($+0.10\ \mathrm{V}$), so it is a better electron donor than $\mathrm{I^-}$ ($E^\circ = +0.54\ \mathrm{V}$).
- **B. Strongest oxidising agent: $\mathrm{I_2}$** (iodine). It is the oxidised form of the couple with the higher $E^\circ$ ($+0.54\ \mathrm{V}$), so it is a better electron acceptor than $\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}$.

**(ii)** The couple with the lower potential is the negative electrode (oxidation, left of the diagram); the couple with the higher potential is the positive electrode (reduction, right).

Cell diagram:

$$\mathrm{Pt} \mid 2\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}(aq)},\ \mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}(aq)} \Vert \mathrm{I_2(aq)},\ 2\mathrm{I^-(aq)} \mid \mathrm{Pt}$$

Cell reaction: $2\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}(aq)} + \mathrm{I_2(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{I^-(aq)}$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{right (positive)}} - E^\circ_{\text{left (negative)}} = (+0.54) - (+0.10) = +0.44\ \mathrm{V}$$

The e.m.f. of the cell is **+0.44 V** (positive, so the reaction is feasible; it is the reaction of an iodine-thiosulphate titration).
